extracted.intended_audience: writers, editors, copyeditors, and students of English grammar and usage
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for correct English grammar and usage covering articles, adjectives, verbs, infinitives, participles, gerunds, voice, mood, and related punctuation/hyphenation rules. Intended to be used when writing, editing, or teaching standard formal prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omitted article and zero article
rubrics_metrics.description: The absence of an article may alter a sentence’s meaning; an article that is implied but omitted is called a zero article, common in idiomatic usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Zero article usually occurs in idiomatic references to time, illness, transportation, personal routines, and meals. Examples: the news brought us little comfort (we weren’t comforted) vs the news brought us a little comfort (we felt somewhat comforted); {by sunset} {has cancer} {travel by train} {go to bed} {make breakfast}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article as pronoun substitute
rubrics_metrics.description: An article may sometimes substitute for a pronoun in contexts where a pronoun or the definite article could both be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example pattern: the blanks in 'a patient who develops the described rash on __ hands should inform __ doctor' may be filled with either a possessive pronoun or the definite article (the).

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic rules for position of adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: An adjective that modifies a noun element usually precedes it (attributive adjective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An adjective may follow the noun (postpositive) if (1) it expresses special emphasis {reasons innumerable}, (2) occurs in standard usage {court-martial}, (3) is a predicate adjective following a linking verb {I am ready}, (4) functions as an appositive set off by commas or dashes {the man, tall and thin, stood...}, or (5) modifies certain pronouns {anything good}. Some adjectives are always predicate; others always attributive. Phrasal adjectives may precede or follow their noun (see adjective phrase).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjective after possessive
rubrics_metrics.description: When a noun phrase includes a possessive noun, the adjective follows the possessive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: children's athletic shoes; the company's former president (unless the intent is athletic children or a former company). Same applies to possessive pronouns: her red dress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjective modifying pronoun
rubrics_metrics.description: When modifying a pronoun, an adjective usually follows the pronoun, sometimes as a predicate adjective; occasionally it may precede.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the searchers found him unconscious; some like it hot; it was insensitive; flustered, he sat down; they offered her the director position but, uncertain, she demurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predicate adjective
rubrics_metrics.description: A predicate adjective follows a linking verb and modifies the subject; it is defined by following a linking verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the child is afraid; this tastes delicious. Distinguish when an adjective in the predicate modifies a different noun in the predicate (then it is not a predicate adjective): 'the train will be here at a late hour' — late modifies hour, not the subject train.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date as adjective
rubrics_metrics.description: Dates used as descriptive adjectives follow particular punctuation/hyphenation conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a month-year or month-day date is used as an adjective, no hyphen or comma is needed {October 31 festivities} {December 2014 financial statement}. A full month-day-year with commas around the year is sometimes used but awkward; better to recast (e.g., 'commencement ceremonies on May 27, 2016').

rubrics_metrics.name: Three degrees of adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives are gradable into positive (absolute), comparative, and superlative degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive expresses quality without comparison {a big balloon}; comparative expresses relation between two items {a cheaper ticket}; superlative denotes extreme among three or more {the biggest house on the block}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative adjectives (synthetic vs periphrastic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparatives show relationship between two things; short adjectives typically use -er (synthetic) and longer adjectives use more (periphrastic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One-syllable adjectives: -er (light-lighter). Three+ syllables: use more/less (more intelligent). Two-syllable adjectives vary; many take more. Two-syllable adjectives ending in -er, -le, -ow, -ure, -y can often use either -er or more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superlative adjectives (synthetic vs periphrastic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Superlatives denote the extreme of intensity among at least three things; short adjectives typically use -est and longer adjectives use most.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One- or two-syllable adjectives often take -est (lighter-lightest); three+ syllables use most (most humorous). Some two-syllable adjectives take -est; most take most.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forming comparatives and superlatives (specific morphological rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules govern forming comparative/superlative suffixes and their exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules include: (1) double final consonant for monosyllables ending vowel+consonant (red-redder-reddest); (2) drop silent -e before suffix (polite-politer); (3) participles used as adjectives require more/most (more boring); (4) a few one-syllable adjectives (real,right,wrong) only take more/most informally; (5) eager, proper, somber take only more/most; (6) two-syllable adjectives with un- prefix can often take suffix or more; (7) many adjectives are irregular (good-better-best); (8) never use both a suffix and more/most (no double comparative 'more greener'). A dictionary shows irregular forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal and unequal comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Higher degrees: -er/-est or more/most; lower degrees: less/least; equivalence: as-as construction or so (usually negative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: cold-less cold; less cold-least cold; 'this is as old as that'; 'that test was not so hard as the last one.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Noncomparable adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives that describe absolute states (entire, impossible, pregnant, unique) are noncomparable and generally cannot take comparatives, superlatives, or intensifiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They cannot be used with more/most or very/quite etc., though rare emphatic departures (e.g., 'more perfect') are historically attested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participial adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Participial adjectives are verb participles functioning as adjectives: present participle (-ing) or past participle (-ed or irregular).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present participle denotes ongoing action {a rising star}; past participle denotes completed action {a completed assignment}. Past participles can be modified by adverbs (quite fatigued, barely concealed) or adverbial phrases (very much distrusted). If the participial form seems more verbal, use 'very much' (very much delayed); if more adjectival, 'very' suffices (very tired). Some participles (bored, interested) are in-between and omit much.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Coordinate adjectives appear in sequence modifying the same noun and should be separated by commas or 'and' when they are coordinate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test: if 'and' can be inserted between adjectives, a comma is necessary. Examples: skilled, experienced chess player vs white brick house (no comma because adjectives are not coordinate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Phrasal adjectives (compound modifiers) and hyphenation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A phrasal adjective (compound modifier) is a phrase functioning as a unit to modify a noun and follows specific hyphenation rules when placed before a noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules include: (1) generally hyphenate before a noun to avoid ambiguity {dog-eat-dog competition}; (2) if a compound noun is an element, hyphenate the entire compound {time-clock-punching employees}; (3) hyphenate when more than one phrasal adjective modifies a noun {nineteenth-century song-and-dance numbers}; (4) use suspended hyphen when phrases share an ending {middle- and upper-class}; (5) drop plural when denoting amount/duration (nine-month pregnancy), except for fractions {a two-thirds majority}; (6) recast if awkward; examples and cross-references provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions for hyphenating phrasal adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain exceptions to hyphenation of phrasal adjectives apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: (1) when the phrasal adjective follows a linking verb it is often unhyphenated (a well-trained athlete vs an athlete who is well trained); (2) when a proper name begins a phrasal adjective the name is not hyphenated {the Monty Python school of comedy}; (3) two-word phrasal adjective beginning with an adverb ending in -ly is not hyphenated {a sharply worded reprimand} (but 'not-so-sharply-worded').

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjectives as nouns (adnoun shift)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some adjectives shift to noun usage (adnouns) and are acceptable when well established, but new or unestablished shifts should be used cautiously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of established shifts: postmortem (for postmortem examination), collectibles, the French. Avoid using adjectives-as-nouns unnecessarily when better alternatives exist (e.g., prefer 'collaboration' to 'a collaborative' used as a noun).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjectives as verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjective-to-verb shifts occur occasionally, generally as jargon or slang, and usually are unsuitable for formal prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'inerted' (jargon), 'low-key the credit' (slang). Use cautiously; they rarely fit formal contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other parts of speech functioning as adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Words that ordinarily belong to other parts of speech (nouns, pronouns, verbs) sometimes function adjectivally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-references to sections on nouns and pronouns; these usages are recognized but governed by standard rules (see other sections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbs generally
rubrics_metrics.description: A verb shows an action, occurrence, condition, or state of being; it is the most essential part of speech and can express a full thought by itself in some contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One-word imperatives can be complete sentences {Run!}. Elliptical one-word responses (Why? Yes) imply omitted clauses and are treated as such.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitive and intransitive verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbs are classified as transitive (require an object) or intransitive (do not require an object).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transitive: 'the cyclist hit a curb' (object curb). Some transitive verbs have cognate objects (drink a drink). Many verbs can be both, with different meanings or no change. Test transitivity by trying objects in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ergative (ambitransitive) verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Ergative verbs can be used transitively or intransitively with the object of the transitive use becoming the subject of the intransitive use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the impact shattered the windshield / the windshield shattered; open: I opened the door / the door opened. Some verbs have shifted uses in commercial/modern usage (ship, grow); caution advised for careful writers and editors—prefer well-established idioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular and irregular verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular verbs form past/past-participle by -ed (or -d); irregular verbs have various patterns (vowel change, same form, different endings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irregular patterns defy simple classification (begin-began-begun; bet-bet-bet). Use a good dictionary for irregulars. Some verbs have alternative past forms ending in -t (dreamt vs dreamed); American English tends to prefer -ed forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linking verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: A linking verb links the subject to a subjective complement and does not take an object because it expresses a state, not an action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two kinds: be-verbs and intransitive verbs used in a weakened sense (appear, become, feel, look, seem, smell, taste). Some verbs occasionally function as linking verbs (act, get, go, grow, lie, prove, remain, sit, stay, turn, wax). A verb is not a linking verb in a construction unless it has a subjective complement (e.g., 'there is an unfilled receptionist position' — be here is existential, not linking).

rubrics_metrics.name: Phrasal verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a preposition or particle functioning as an adverb; it is not hyphenated even if equivalent noun/adjective forms might be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three guiding rules: (1) if the phrasal verb has a distinct meaning, use the whole phrase (hold up = rob/delay); (2) avoid the phrasal verb if the single verb conveys the meaning (rest up vs rest); (3) don't compress the phrase into a one-word verb especially when a one-word noun form exists (burns out vs burnout). Examples: settle down, act up, phase out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal and auxiliary verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: A principal verb can stand alone to express an act or state; an auxiliary verb combines with a principal to form verbal phrases that indicate mood, tense, or voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of auxiliaries: be, can, do, have, may, must, ought, shall, will. Principal verb is the leading thought when combined (a tiger may roar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Verb phrases (auxiliary + principal) and modifier placement
rubrics_metrics.description: A verb phrase combines an auxiliary with a principal verb; adverbial modifiers typically follow the first auxiliary; verb phrases can be split and negated after the first auxiliary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: could certainly happen; must always go; will soon be leaving. Negation: we have not called him. Interrogatives place the first auxiliary before the subject: must I repeat that? Contractions are common and natural in many contexts (don't you want more?).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractions usage guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Most types of writing benefit from the use of contractions when used thoughtfully, making prose sound natural and relaxed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common contractions: aren't, wasn't, can't, couldn't, don't, won't, hasn't, hasn't. Avoid awkward/rare contractions (oughtn't) except perhaps in dialogue. Some contractions are ambiguous (there's = there is/there has; I'd = I had/I would). Use caution with less common contractions (I'd've, she'd've).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinitives defined
rubrics_metrics.description: An infinitive is the verb's root or stem in uninflected form, often preceded by to (the sign of the infinitive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To is sometimes classed as adverb. In active voice, to is generally dropped when the infinitive follows an auxiliary (you must flee) and can be dropped after certain verbs (bid, dare, feel, hear, help, let, make, need, see) in active voice. In passive voice after these verbs, retain to (he cannot be heard to deny it). Retain to after ought/ought not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uses of the infinitive
rubrics_metrics.description: Infinitives are versatile: they act as part of verb phrases, as nouns, adjectives, or adverbs and can take subjects, objects, predicate complements, or adverbial modifiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As verb: can take subject (we wanted the lesson to end), object (try to throw the javelin higher), predicate complement (want to race home?), adverbial modifier (you need to think quickly). As noun: subject of a verb (to fly is a lofty goal) or object of a verb (I want to hire...). An infinitive may be governed by a verb, noun, adjective, participle, or pronoun.

rubrics_metrics.name: Split infinitive
rubrics_metrics.description: Placement of adverbs between to and the verb is now widely acknowledged as sometimes justifiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: they expect to more than double their income next year. Historical prescriptive bans are relaxed where clarity or emphasis requires the split.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangling infinitive
rubrics_metrics.description: An infinitive phrase used to modify a verb must have a logical subject capable of performing the infinitive's action; otherwise the infinitive is dangling and the sentence may be confusing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poor: To repair your car properly, it must be sent to a mechanic (no logical subject for repair). Better: To repair your car properly, you must take it to a mechanic. Revise to provide a logical subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participles generally
rubrics_metrics.description: Participles are nonfinite verb forms with tense: present participle ends in -ing (action in progress) and past participle usually ends in -ed (action completed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present participle example: watching intently for a mouse, the cat settled in to wait. Past participle example: planted in the spring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participial phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: A participial phrase consists of a participle plus associated words and can function as an adjective modifying a noun/pronoun or as an absolute phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: nailed to the roof, the slate stopped the leaks (adjectival); generally speaking, I prefer spicy dishes (absolute). Cross-ref: participial adjectives section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gerunds
rubrics_metrics.description: A gerund is a present participle used as a noun and can function as subject, object, predicate nominative, or object of a preposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Complaining about it won't help (subject). I don't like your cooking (object). His favorite pastime is sleeping (predicate nominative). Reduce erosion by terracing the fields (object of preposition). Gerunds may substitute for infinitives in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing between participles and gerunds
rubrics_metrics.description: Although both derive from verbs, participles function as modifiers or part of verb phrases and are modified by adverbs; gerunds function as nouns and are modified by adjectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: participle — the swiftly running water; gerund — sporadic running and walking makes for a great workout (gerund modified by adjective 'sporadic').

rubrics_metrics.name: Fused participles (gerund modification by pronouns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a nonpossessive noun or pronoun to 'modify' a gerund (a fused participle) is traditionally considered a fault; possessive forms are preferred where idiomatic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: POOR: Me painting your fence depends on you paying me first. BETTER: My painting your fence depends on your paying me first. Exceptions occur where possessive is unidiomatic (nonpersonal nouns/pronouns or group pronouns) — forced fused participles are tolerated in those cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangling participles
rubrics_metrics.description: A participle that has no syntactic relationship with the nearest subject (dangling participle) results in illogical, ambiguous, or incoherent sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Frequently used in early America, experts suggest...' (used modifies shaming not experts). Fix by recasting so the participle is associated with the correct noun: 'experts suggest that shaming, often used in early America, is an effective punishment.' Passive-voice independent clauses can produce danglers; prefer active voice or recast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangling gerunds
rubrics_metrics.description: A dangling gerund occurs when a participle used as a noun (gerund) lacks a clear logical actor, causing ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: After finishing the research, the screenplay was easy to write (who finished?). Revise: After Gero finished the research, the screenplay was easy to write, or After finishing the research, Gero found the screenplay easy to write. Avoid improbable statements (While driving to San Antonio, my phone ran out of power) by clarifying the gerund's subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five properties of verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbs have five properties: voice, mood, tense, person, and number; verbs are conjugated to show these properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a framework for subsequent rules on voice, mood, tense, person, and number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active and passive voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Voice shows whether the subject performs the action (active) or receives it (passive); passive voice is formed with an inflected form of 'be' (or colloquially 'get') plus the past participle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active: the judge levied a $50 fine. Passive: the tree’s branch was broken by the storm. Passive is typically, though not always, inferior to active style; choose voice to suit desired point of view (mouse was caught by the cat vs the cat caught the mouse). Note: presence of a be-verb alone does not indicate passive (he is thinking is not passive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive conjugation and voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Progressive conjugation uses an inflected form of be plus a present participle (is pulling); combining be-verbs with a past participle can produce passive progressive constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a verb phrase is transitive and uses be + present participle, it's progressive active {the ox is pulling the cart}. If be-verbs + past participle occur (the cart is being pulled) the result is passive voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verb mood — indicative
rubrics_metrics.description: The indicative mood expresses facts and opinions and asks questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: amethysts cost very little; the botanist lives in a garden cottage; does that bush produce yellow roses?

rubrics_metrics.name: Verb mood — imperative
rubrics_metrics.description: The imperative mood expresses commands, direct requests, and sometimes permission; the subject 'you' is understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Go away! Bring the tray in here. Use imperatives cautiously as they can be blunt; soften with 'please' or recast as a polite indicative question (Will you stop at the store, please?).
